content: Ankle pain and swelling are common clinical issues that can arise due to either acute or chronic injuries or degenerative conditions. The most frequent cause of ankle pain is an ankle sprain, which typically results from a traumatic inversion injury. If swelling is present in both ankles, it may suggest systemic causes such as cardiac or vascular conditions rather than a localized problem within the foot or ankle. Differential Diagnosis The potential causes of ankle pain and swelling include: An avulsion fracture of the distal fibula, where a fragment of bone is pulled away by a ligament or tendon. Bimalleolar fractures, involving both the medial and lateral malleoli. Degenerative joint disease, which can lead to chronic pain and stiffness. Diabetic arthropathy (Charcot's joint), a complication of diabetes that results in joint destruction. Inversion sprains, caused by the inward rolling of the ankle. Injuries to the subtalar joint due to inversion or eversion forces. Neoplasms, which may present as a mass or pain in the ankle region. Entrapment of the peroneal nerve, leading to pain or sensory changes. Poorly aligned footwear, which can contribute to repetitive strain injuries. Recurrent injuries that disrupt the ankle retinaculum, a fibrous structure stabilizing the tendons. Syndesmosis injuries, which involve the ligaments connecting the tibia and fibula. Trimalleolar fractures, involving the medial malleolus, lateral malleolus, and posterior tibial margin. Physical Examination A thorough physical examination is essential and should include: Inspection and palpation of the ankle, foot, and lower leg. Assessment of pulses to evaluate vascular supply. Evaluation of neurovascular status, including sensation and motor function. Observation of skin color and capillary refill to assess circulation. Imaging Studies X-rays: The Ottawa ankle rules help determine the need for imaging after trauma. Indications for an ankle x-ray include: Tenderness at the proximal fifth metatarsal. Tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the fibula or tibia. Tenderness in the navicular area. Inability to bear weight for at least four steps. Standard imaging includes lateral, oblique, and anteroposterior (AP) views. Stress views, foot series, or lower leg series may also be required. MRI and CT: These advanced imaging modalities are used when further evaluation is necessary, such as for soft tissue injuries or complex fractures. Other Diagnostic Studies The anterior and posterior drawer tests assess ligament stability. Range of motion and muscle strength testing are critical for functional evaluation. Treatment The management of ankle pain and swelling can be summarized using the mnemonic PRINCE: Protection: Prevent further injury by immobilizing the ankle if needed. Rest: Avoid activities that exacerbate symptoms. Ice: Apply cold therapy to reduce swelling and inflammation. NSAIDs: Use nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs to manage pain and inflammation. Compression: Apply an elastic bandage or wrap to control swelling. Elevation: Keep the ankle elevated to reduce edema. Additional treatment options include: Casting, if immobilization is required for healing. Physical therapy to restore range of motion and improve muscle strength. Surgery and Device-Based Therapy Ankle bracing or foot orthoses can help prevent reinjury and provide support during recovery. Surgical intervention may be necessary for specific fractures or severe ligament injuries that do not respond to conservative management.
